hero.title: Some Types of Alloys Used in the Iraqi Setting
hero.lead: From old Iraqi metal coins to stainless steel in power stations: learn in this lesson about examples of alloys close to our Iraqi setting.

objectives: States types of alloys used in the Iraqi setting along with their places of use.
Explains why iron's hardness increases when carbon is added to it to form steel.

content.heading: 💡 8-8 Some Types of Alloys Used in the Iraqi Setting
content.html: Alloys are part of many details close to our daily life in Iraq, from old metal coins to petroleum-industry equipment and household tools.

content.svgAriaLabel: Simulation of Iraqi metal coin alloys
content.sectionHeading: 🕹️ Interactive Simulation: Iraqi Metal Coins and Their Alloys
content.descriptionHtml: Press any coin to learn about the alloy it is made of.

labels.c5Text: The 5-fils coin: its alloy is made up of copper and nickel in a specific ratio and weight.
labels.c10Text: The 10-fils coin: its alloy is made up of copper and nickel in a specific ratio and weight, heavier than the 5-fils coin.
labels.c25Text: The 25-fils coin: its alloy is made up of silver and copper in equal ratios and weights.

content.label: 🔢 Enumeration — Some Types of Alloys in the Iraqi Setting
listItems: Alloys were used in minting coins, as was in circulation in Iraq some years ago, such as: the 5-fils coin, made up of copper and nickel in a specific ratio and weight; the 10-fils coin, also made up of copper and nickel in a specific ratio and weight; and the 25-fils coin, whose alloy is made up of silver and copper in equal ratios and weights.
Lead alloy, which is used in manufacturing solder, liquid batteries, hydraulic presses, and printing type.
Stainless steel, an alloy used widely in electrical power generation stations, the petroleum industry, chemical industries, and for use in household utensils and equipment.

content.html: In its pure state, iron is softer than aluminum, and its hardness increases when alloying elements such as carbon are added in specific proportions, forming steel alloy, which is a thousand times stronger than pure iron.

summary.heading: 📋 Lesson Summary
items: Copper-nickel alloys were used in the 5- and 10-fils coins, and silver-copper alloy in the 25-fils coin, in Iraq previously.
Lead alloy is used in solder, liquid batteries, hydraulic presses, and printing type.
Stainless steel is used widely in power generation stations, the petroleum and chemical industries, and household tools.
Adding carbon in specific proportions to pure iron (softer than aluminum) forms steel alloy, a thousand times stronger than pure iron.
